title: How does sealing interact with generics and wildcards?
shortTitle: How does sealing interact with generics and wildcards?

s1_definition.profdef: A sealed type can be generic, and its permitted subtypes can specialize or keep the type parameter, so you can model a closed set of alternatives that each carry typed data. Sealing applies to the raw/generic class as a type declaration, independent of the specific type arguments, because generics are erased at runtime while the `PermittedSubclasses` attribute records the closed set of subtype classes. Wildcards (`? extends`, `? super`) work normally on a sealed generic type, and exhaustive pattern matching still holds across the closed set regardless of the wildcard used, though the compiler reasons about exhaustiveness at the level of the sealed classes, not the individual type arguments.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India having a sealed, closed set of "typed order tickets": a BuyOrder and a SellOrder, where each ticket is stamped with the kind of instrument it trades — equity, bond, or currency. The sealed rule fixes that there are exactly two ticket shapes (Buy and Sell). The generic type parameter is the instrument stamp on the ticket. A wildcard like "any order of some instrument" is like a clerk saying "give me any order ticket regardless of which instrument it trades" — they can read common fields but cannot stamp a new instrument blindly. The closed set of two ticket shapes stays closed no matter which instrument stamp is on them.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sealing closes the set of subtype classes while generics parameterize the data each carries, so the closed set and exhaustive matching hold regardless of type arguments or wildcards.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A sealed type can be generic, and its permitted subtypes can specialize or keep the type parameter, so you can model a closed set of alternatives that each carry typed data. Sealing applies to the raw/generic class as a type declaration, independent of the specific type arguments, because generics are erased at runtime while the `PermittedSubclasses` attribute records the closed set of subtype classes. Wildcards (`? extends`, `? super`) work normally on a sealed generic type, and exhaustive pattern matching still holds across the closed set regardless of the wildcard used, though the compiler reasons about exhaustiveness at the level of the sealed classes, not the individual type arguments.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India having a sealed, closed set of "typed order tickets": a BuyOrder and a SellOrder, where each ticket is stamped with the kind of instrument it trades — equity, bond, or currency. The sealed rule fixes that there are exactly two ticket shapes (Buy and Sell). The generic type parameter is the instrument stamp on the ticket. A wildcard like "any order of some instrument" is like a clerk saying "give me any order ticket regardless of which instrument it trades" — they can read common fields but cannot stamp a new instrument blindly. The closed set of two ticket shapes stays closed no matter which instrument stamp is on them.

**One line to remember:** Sealing closes the set of subtype classes while generics parameterize the data each carries, so the closed set and exhaustive matching hold regardless of type arguments or wildcards.

sections.s2_technical:
A sealed interface can declare a type parameter: `sealed interface Order<T extends Instrument> permits BuyOrder, SellOrder`. Each permitted subtype decides how to handle the parameter. It can stay generic, like `final class BuyOrder<T extends Instrument> implements Order<T>`, or it can fix the parameter, like `final class SellOrder<T extends Instrument> implements Order<T>`, or a subtype could even bind it to a concrete type such as `final class EquityBuyOrder implements Order<Equity>`. The sealing constraint is about which classes may extend, listed in `permits`, and that list names classes, not parameterized types. Because generics are erased, the `PermittedSubclasses` attribute stores the subtype classes, and the closed set is defined at the class level.

Wildcards behave exactly as they do for any generic type. You can write a method parameter `Order<? extends Instrument> order` to accept any order of any instrument, and you can write `Order<? super Equity>` for contravariant needs. For example `BigDecimal notional(Order<? extends Instrument> order)` can read common behavior through the `Order` interface. A key point for pattern matching: an exhaustive `switch` over `Order<? extends Instrument>` still only needs to cover `BuyOrder` and `SellOrder`, because exhaustiveness is checked against the closed set of permitted classes, not against the possible type arguments. For example `switch (order) { case BuyOrder<?> b -> ...; case SellOrder<?> s -> ...; }` is exhaustive with no default.

There are senior nuances. First, when you pattern-match a generic sealed type you usually match with a wildcard pattern like `case BuyOrder<?> b`, because the exact type argument is erased and generally not recoverable at runtime. Second, bounded type parameters on the sealed type propagate to the permitted subtypes so the whole hierarchy shares the bound, which is useful for keeping a domain like `T extends Instrument` consistent. Third, sealing plus generics is a clean way to build type-safe heterogeneous results, such as a sealed `Result<T>` with `Success<T>` and `Failure<T>`, giving you exhaustive handling of success and failure while carrying a typed payload. Finally, variance choices still belong to the use site via wildcards; sealing does not change variance, it only closes the subtype set.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's trading desk places orders on different instrument types, but every order is still exactly one of two actions: Buy or Sell. The bank wants a closed set of order actions while each order carries a strongly typed instrument. This is exactly how a generic sealed interface works — the sealed part closes the Buy/Sell set, and the type parameter carries the instrument type safely.

Problem 2 — A risk function must accept any order of any instrument to compute its notional value, reading common fields without caring about the exact instrument type. This is exactly what a wildcard like `Order<? extends Instrument>` is for — it accepts the whole family while the exhaustive switch over the closed Buy/Sell set still needs no default.

The demo defines a generic sealed interface `Order<T extends Instrument>`, two permitted generic classes `BuyOrder` and `SellOrder`, an `Instrument` hierarchy with `Equity`, builds orders for Rajesh and Priya, and computes notional via a wildcard-typed method using an exhaustive switch. Classes and steps: `Instrument` (interface), `Equity` (record), `Order<T>` (sealed interface), `BuyOrder<T>`/`SellOrder<T>` (permitted classes), `RiskEngine` (wildcard method + exhaustive switch), and `BankDemo` (main).

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Reliance equity priced Rs.2,450.50; Rajesh (SAV2001) buys 100 shares; Priya (CUR3001) sells 40 shares.

Step 1 — Both orders are created as `Order<Equity>`. The sealed interface closes the action set to Buy and Sell, and the type parameter pins each order to the `Equity` instrument.

Step 2 — The orders are placed into a `List<Order<? extends Instrument>>`. The wildcard lets the list hold any instrument family while still being an `Order`.

Step 3 — `RiskEngine.notional` accepts the wildcard-typed order and calls `grossValue` through the interface. For Rajesh it computes 2,450.50 times 100 equals Rs.245,050. For Priya it computes 2,450.50 times 40 equals Rs.98,020.

Step 4 — `RiskEngine.action` runs an exhaustive switch over the closed set using wildcard patterns `BuyOrder<?>` and `SellOrder<?>`. No default is needed because the sealed set has exactly two classes. Rajesh's order matches Buy, Priya's matches Sell.

```
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [INFO] Notional = Rs.245050.00 | BUY 100 RELIANCE for SAV2001
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [INFO] Notional = Rs.98020.00 | SELL 40 RELIANCE for CUR3001
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Sealing and generics work together cleanly because they constrain different things. Sealing closes the set of subtype classes that may extend a type, and that permits list names classes, not parameterized types. Generics parameterize the data each subtype carries. So I can declare a generic sealed interface, give it a bounded type parameter, and let each permitted subtype either keep the parameter, fix it, or bind it to a concrete type. Because generics are erased and the permitted-subclasses metadata records classes, the closed set is defined at the class level and is completely independent of the specific type arguments.

In my trading work at National Bank of India I modeled orders as a generic sealed interface Order of T where T is bounded to Instrument, with exactly two permitted subtypes, BuyOrder and SellOrder, each keeping the type parameter. Rajesh places a buy order for Reliance equity and Priya places a sell order, and both are typed as Order of Equity, so the instrument stays strongly typed all the way through. My risk engine accepts orders using a wildcard, Order of some extends Instrument, so it can process any order of any instrument and read the gross value through the interface without needing the exact type argument.

The important interaction for pattern matching is that an exhaustive switch over that wildcard-typed order still only needs to cover BuyOrder and SellOrder, with no default branch, because exhaustiveness is checked against the closed set of permitted classes and not against the possible type arguments. In practice I match with wildcard patterns like BuyOrder of question-mark, because the type argument is erased at runtime. This gives me compiler-checked handling of every order action while keeping the instrument data type-safe at the API boundary.

So in an interview I summarize it as: sealing closes the family of classes, generics type the payload they carry, and wildcards let me consume the whole family at the use site. The closed set and the exhaustive switch hold regardless of type arguments, which is exactly why a generic sealed hierarchy like a Result of T or an Order of T is such a strong, type-safe modeling tool.
